A traveler paused by a river and told a short story to the wind. The water kept moving, and the next morning a child on the far bank repeated the tale in a new voice. Nobody in the valley knew how the words had crossed the wide current during the night, yet every villager who walked down to the stone pier before dawn swore that the mist itself seemed to hum with a quiet, unfamiliar melody.

The traveler, whose name was Julian, carried an old leather satchel filled with notebooks bound in faded blue linen. For seven years he had walked from the salt marshes of the southern coast to the high cedar ridges of the north, collecting stories that people only remembered when the lamps were burned low. He was not a scholar from the capital, nor was he a merchant looking for rare goods. He simply believed that stories were like seeds carried by migratory birds: if they stayed in one courtyard forever, they eventually lost their strength, but if they were spoken aloud near moving water, they found their way to soil where they were needed most.

That evening, the autumn air had turned crisp, and the lanterns of Oakhaven glimmered across the river like fallen stars floating on dark glass. Because the wooden ferry had been tied up for repairs after a late summer storm, Julian could not cross to the village. Instead, he built a small fire of driftwood on the eastern shingle, brewed a pot of wild mint tea, and sat with his back against an ancient willow tree. As the embers settled into a steady orange glow, he opened his seventh notebook and began to read aloud to the rushing water.
